name: Erik Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm foreman for the coast district, so it's the town, the harbour and the beach road out to the point. A normal day, I meet the crew at the yard at seven, we go through the jobs, and the big one most weeks is salt. The sea air eats the hardware, so we're always swapping corroded clamps and insulators before they fail. I like the crew, we're like family, and I like that people wave at the truck. What wears me out is the winter storms coming off the sea, when we're out all night in the rain.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the volunteer fire brigade, twenty-two years now. My wife Rosa runs the church office three days a week. Our daughter got married last year and we paid for most of it, and our grandson Leo, he's nine, has been living with us since his mum went through a hard time. My son showed me one of those AI programs and I use it now and then to tidy up my safety talks, but I don't lean on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, the old ways still work. At the yard we'd have a laugh, and at the fire station too. I'm not online much, so that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on, and I'm fine with that. Money's tight but it's always been tight, and that's on us, not on computers. We made our choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Work, the brigade, church on Sunday. Keep chipping away at the credit card from the wedding, and try to put something aside for Leo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad things stay as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the wedding. How's the money now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We put the wedding on a card and an advance from my pension fund, which I probably shouldn't have done. So we've got less than a month of money and a card to pay down. But she only gets married once, and I'd do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Leo? Does he change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He does. I thought at this age it'd be me and Rosa, a little trip now and then. Now it's school runs and football on Saturdays, and I wouldn't change it, but I need to keep working to 66 at least.

S0.say: I'd say the old ways still work and have a laugh about it at the yard and the fire station. I'm not online much, so that's about it.
S0.think: Privately I carry on and I'm fine with that. Money's always been tight, and that's on us, not on computers.
S0.do: Carries on with work, the fire brigade and church. Keeps paying down the wedding credit card and tries to save a little for his grandson.
S0.feel: Calm and glad things stay as they are.
S0.quote: But she only gets married once, and I'd do it again.
S0.fieldNote: Erik takes responsibility for his tight finances himself, mentioning the wedding and pension advance. Raising his grandson means he needs to work to at least 66. He's settled in community and church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we adapt, like we always have. Nobody owes us a living, but a good company looks after its people and trains them. I'd say that at work and at the brigade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine, but I'm not sure. I'm the foreman and I know every pole in the district. But if they bring in robots for the corrosion work, they'll need fewer of us, and 58 is not a good age to be the one let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the new kit had been tried on a couple of jobs, then put my hand up to learn it. In the first year I'd want the company to set up proper training, like an apprenticeship for the new stuff. I'd keep paying down the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to see it proven. What would you watch for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether it works in salt air and wind, because a lot of things don't. If the robots are still running after a winter on the beach road, then I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the yard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones, Josh and Kai, both on their first years. They need someone to teach them by hand. If the robots do the work, who teaches them?

S1.say: I'd say we adapt as we always have. Nobody owes us a living, but a good company trains and looks after its people.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd probably be fine as foreman, but I'm not sure. Robots for corrosion work would mean fewer crew, and 58 is a bad age to be let go.
S1.do: Waits until new equipment has been tried on real jobs, then volunteers to learn it. Asks the company for apprenticeship-style training on new kit and keeps paying down his credit card.
S1.quote: If the robots are still running after a winter on the beach road, then I'd believe it.
S1.fieldNote: Erik mixes self-reliance with an expectation that a good employer trains its people. He wants proof in real salt-air conditions. His concern goes straight to the young apprentices and who will teach them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three pictures about full AGI, at different speeds. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being forced on people too fast, and the companies building this are going to wreck a lot of families. I'd want our leaders to slow it down. I'd say it at the brigade and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's bad for us. I'd be 60, with a card to pay and less than a month of money, and Leo to raise. If robots can do the corrosion work and the storm work, I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything down that week: no trips, no takeaway, the card first. I'd ask our son and daughter if they could help with Leo's costs for a while. I'd look for any work in town, even outside the grid, maybe at the harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. And ashamed, a bit, that I didn't save more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're going to be fine and that Grandpa's going to find something. I'd keep his routine the same, school, football. Kids need things to stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you look for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The harbour, maybe, or the fire service if they're hiring paid crew. But the robots would be coming there too, wouldn't they? I don't know.

S2.say: I'd say it's being forced on people too fast and the companies building it will wreck a lot of families. I'd want leaders to slow it down.
S2.think: Privately it's bad for us: I'd be 60 with a card to pay, less than a month of money and my grandson to raise. If robots can do corrosion and storm work, I'm out.
S2.do: Cuts spending that week, starting with the credit card. Asks his grown children to help with his grandson's costs and looks for any work in town, such as at the harbour.
S2.feel: Frightened, and a little ashamed he didn't save more.
S2.quote: Frightened, honestly. And ashamed, a bit, that I didn't save more.
S2.fieldNote: Raising his grandson raises the stakes of a fast shock. He blames himself for not saving more and the tech firms for the speed. He'd lean on family before government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's get ready. I'd push the company to train us and keep the apprentices on. I'd say it calmer than with the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63, so not far from my pension. If I could hang on as the one who checks the robots' work, I'd make it. It'd be tight, but I could see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the card off over the first two years and start a little savings. Once the robots had been tested, I'd get trained on them. I'd also look at the brigade, because they might still need people with local know-how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. It feels like a storm warning rather than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Rosa and work out a budget, and talk to the company about what training they plan. Then pay the card off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd wait to see it proven. Can you afford to wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year. I'd give it a year to see the robots work, then move. Waiting longer would be foolish.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's get ready. I'd push the company to train us and keep apprentices on.
S3.think: Privately I'd be 63 and close to my pension. If I could stay on checking robots' work, I'd make it, though it would be tight.
S3.do: Pays off the credit card over two years and starts saving. Gets trained on robots once tested, after giving it about a year, and looks at whether the fire brigade still needs local know-how.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, like a storm warning instead of a storm.
S3.quote: It feels like a storm warning rather than a storm.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him use his wait-then-move habit, with a clear one-year limit. Paying off the card is his first priority. He still sees the fire brigade as part of his future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people work for it. I'd tell young people to learn a trade, the robots will need fixing. I'd say it at the brigade and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be retired, so it's Leo I think about. He'd be 19, starting out right when this arrives. That's what keeps me thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as normal, learn the new kit once it's tried and pay the card off. I'd save what I could for Leo's training. And I'd talk to him about what to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for Leo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leo would be 19 by then. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want him to get an apprenticeship, or a trade the robots can't take. Maybe working with the robots, fixing them. I'd want to save enough to help him get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And for you, at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retired, God willing, with Rosa, maybe a little fishing. The brigade until they kick me out. I'd be all right.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people work for it. I'd tell young people to learn a trade because the robots will need fixing.
S4.think: Privately I'd be retired, so it's my grandson Leo I think about. He'd be 19, starting out right as this arrives.
S4.do: Keeps working as normal, learns new kit once tested and pays off the card. Saves what he can for his grandson's training and talks with him about what to study.
S4.quote: Retired, God willing, with Rosa, maybe a little fishing. The brigade until they kick me out.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Erik's own future looks fine and the worry shifts to his grandson, who'd be starting out just as AGI lands. He keeps coming back to trades and apprenticeships. His self-reliant outlook stays constant.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be 60 with less than a month of money, a card to pay and Leo to raise. What would help is the company keeping on people who know the district to check the robots' work, and proper training, run like an apprenticeship, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens on a storm night. When the sea comes over the beach road and the poles go down, you need people who know which house has an old lady on her own. A robot doesn't know the town.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't know the town.
portrait: Erik Garcia is a 58-year-old foreman for a coastal district who spends his days fighting salt corrosion and his spare time on the volunteer fire brigade. A daughter's wedding and raising his nine-year-old grandson Leo have left him with less than a month of savings and a credit card to pay down. He takes the blame for that himself and believes in adapting and apprenticeships. He's calm about a plateau and uneasy about steady change, wanting robots proven in salt air first. Fast AGI frightens him because of Leo, while five or ten years gives him room to wait, train and move, and his worry shifts to Leo's future.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be 60 with less than a month of money, a credit card to pay and his grandson to raise.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping people who know the district to check the robots' work, and proper apprenticeship-style training rather than handouts.
